You are checking one scene of a novel for one specific continuity error.

The book had already established this, earlier or elsewhere:
- (journals-of-the-east-wing) "Eleven years since Ryn left."

A past rewrite of this scene contradicted it. The error looked like this:
- (journals-of-the-east-wing) "Ryn had initiated him into the Hold's daily rhythms during his own first weeks, three years ago."
(Summary: Bren says Ryn showed him the Hold's routines in his first weeks three years ago; the same scene says Ryn left eleven years ago.)

Here is a NEW draft of the same scene:
<scene>
The door to the east wing hadn't been opened in years. Bren could tell by the way the latch fought him, the iron gone stiff with cold and disuse, and by the breath of air that came out when it finally gave — stale, dry, the smell of a room that had stopped expecting anyone.

He held the lamp up. The corridor ran straight back into the dark, doors on both sides, all of them shut. His light reached the first few and no further.

He told himself he was here for a reason. Ivra had said, two nights ago at the table, that the old chambers in the east were used for storage now. He'd asked storage of what. She'd shrugged in that way she had, the shrug that meant she knew and wasn't going to say until he'd done the asking himself.

The floorboards complained under his boots. He opened the first door.

An empty chamber. Bed frame against the wall, stripped of everything that made a bed. A desk. A window with the shutter half-rotted. Someone had lived here once, had slept in that frame and sat at that desk and looked out that window at the peaks. Now there was nothing to say who. He crossed to the desk and ran his fingers along the top. The dust came up in a clean line.

He did this to himself sometimes — found a thing and couldn't stop following it. His mother had called it stubbornness. He stepped back into the corridor and kept going.

The second room was the same. The third. In the fourth, the floorboards near the window had worn down to a paler color, a shallow groove the length of two strides, where a person had walked the same line back and forth enough times to carve it. Bren stood in it. He put his boots where the other boots had gone. Four steps to the window, four steps back. He thought about how many times you'd have to make that walk to leave a mark in stone-hard wood, and then he stopped thinking about it, because the number got large fast and he didn't like where it went.

He kept going.

At the end of the corridor the last door opened onto a larger room. A common room, he guessed, from the long-dead hearth and the benches shoved against one wall. And against the other wall, stacked three and four high, the crates.

He counted them before he meant to. He always counted. There were more than he wanted there to be.

He set the lamp on the nearest crate and pried the lid. Nails that had rusted into their holes. The wood split before it let go, and inside, packed tight, were journals. Leather-bound, warped, some with the spines cracked, some wrapped in oilcloth against the damp. He lifted one out. The leather was cold as the stone.

He opened it to the first page.

*Today I Held for the first time. The Rend is nothing like they described in training. They give you the flame and the wind. They don't tell you the wind has a shape. They don't tell you it knows where to push.*

No name on the cover. A date at the top of the entry — he did the arithmetic without wanting to. Forty years back. He turned the pages. The hand was neat at first, young, the letters sitting square on their lines. The entries came close together, then further apart.

*I am twenty-three years old and I have volunteered to let something eat me. I knew that when I signed. I did not know it the way I know it now, with the thing in the room.*

Bren was twenty-six. He'd been three years at Thornwall. He set the journal on his knee and pressed his palm flat against the page, as if he could hold the words still, and read on.

The entries thinned toward the back. The hand got harder to read, not from age but from something gone slack in it. One of the last said: *I forgot how to cry and didn't notice until I tried. There was a reason to and I reached for it and the reaching found nothing. I wrote it here so that when I read it back I would at least have the fact of it.* Below that, two more entries, short, functional. Then blank pages to the end.

He closed the journal. His hands weren't steady. He put it down and picked up the next.

A different hand. The same beginning. Not the same words, but close enough that his skin went cold — a young person, first session, surprise at how little the training matched the thing itself. Then the slow narrowing. One of them kept records of what they'd lost, a list that grew down the margins over years. *My sister's name for me. The taste of the orchard. The word for a color I used to know.* The list stopped partway down a page. He didn't know whether that meant the losses stopped or the noticing did.

He went through the first crate and started the second. The lamp was the only warmth in the room. His breath showed when he leaned toward the light.

The journals didn't agree on everything. Some wrote lyrically, some flat, some only kept the official log and let the personal pages fill with weather and complaints about the food. But under all of it, the same shape. A person arrived whole. A person was spent. And every few years, near the back of whatever book held their last entry, the same note in a dozen hands: *The fissure is stronger than they class it. I have written to Verath. The request was denied.*

Someone had seen it every generation. Someone had put it on paper and sent it down the mountain and gotten the paper back with a stamp on it. The official forms recorded sessions and durations and nothing underneath. These recorded the underneath. The two had been running side by side for sixty years and the one that mattered had stayed in the dark in crates while the other one went to Verath and came home denied.

He was into the fourth crate when he found the recent ones. The leather less cracked, the ink less faded. He knew the dates before he read them.

The journal he opened last had a hand he almost recognized. He read a line and understood why.

*Three of us left after Marren. Torren is here but Torren is mostly not. The new Warden took the posting from Ashward and no one at Ashward could tell me why a man would ask for Thornwall. I asked him. He said the fissure needed someone who wouldn't leave. I don't think he knows yet what it is he won't be leaving.*

Bren turned the page.

*Kael is staying. He'll hold this place together or it will break him. I have seen men try to hold a failing Hold and I have seen what it does. I would tell him to go. He would not go. There is no point in the telling. I am writing it here instead, so that it is written somewhere that I knew.*

The entry was dated eleven years ago. There were only a few pages after it, and then the book was done.

Bren sat on the cold floor of the common room with the journal open on his knees and did not read the last pages. He didn't need to. He'd read eleven of these now and he knew how they ended. He'd watched Torren eat his supper with the slow care of a man counting out the one sense he had left. He'd watched Kael come up from the chamber in the morning with something gone out of him that he never named.

The number he'd been pushing away came back and this time he let it. Three years. He'd given three. The journals around him averaged — he'd been doing the arithmetic the whole time without admitting it — they averaged out to fifteen or twenty, and here was a room that said the fissure was never what they called it, and the shortfall between what it was and what they called it got paid in these books, in these hands going slack, year after year, with the proof sitting sealed in the dark where no one would ever be asked to look.

He got to his feet. His legs had gone stiff from the cold floor. He gathered the recent journals first, the ones with the newer leather, then went back for the oldest — the one that began forty years ago with a young hand and ended with a person who forgot how to cry. He stacked them into the crook of his arm as many as he could carry, blew out the lamp, and carried them back down the corridor past the stripped rooms and the worn groove in the floor, out through the door that fought him again on the way closed.

---

Ivra was in the records room, where she always was in the mornings, logbooks open in front of her and a pot of something gone cold at her elbow. She looked up when he came in and took in the stack in his arms before he'd said a word.

"The east wing," he said. He set the journals down on her table, harder than he meant to. "Sixty-three years of personal records. They're all saying the same thing."

She didn't reach for them. She looked at them for a long moment, and then she looked at him.

"I knew what I'd find," he said. "I walked in there thinking I knew. The fissure's underclassed, we've known that since the inspection. But knowing is different from proving." He put his hand flat on the top journal, the way he had in the dark. "This is the proof. It's been the proof for sixty years."

"How many crates?" Ivra asked.

"I didn't count all of them." That was a lie. He'd counted. He told her the number.

She nodded slowly, as if it confirmed something. She pulled the top journal toward her and opened it, and he watched her read, watched her face not change, which with Ivra was the same as any other person going white.

"You knew these were here," he said. It wasn't a question.

"I knew the crates were here." She turned a page. "When they close a Hold, they send wagons for the furniture. They don't send anyone for the records. I learned that at Garren's Watch. I carried three decades of it out myself in a trunk and not one person asked me what was in it." She turned another page. "When I transferred here I found Thornwall's already boxed. I never opened them. I didn't want to know how many there were."

"There are a lot of them."

"Yes."

He pulled out the chair across from her and sat. The warmth of the records room was getting into his hands again, and with it the shaking came back worse, now that there was nothing to carry.

"Someone wrote to Verath every few years," he said. "Every generation, near the end, they'd write and say the fissure's stronger than the class. And every time it came back denied. It's in the books. The dates line up. You could put the denials next to the entries and show it."

Ivra reached under the table and took out a fresh logbook, blank, and set it between them. She uncapped her ink.

"Then that's what we'll do," she said. "Every crate. Every entry. Dates, names where there are names, the losses where they recorded them. Next to the official log for the same year." She wrote a heading across the top of the first page and underlined it with one flat stroke. "The forms Verath keeps say nothing. These say everything. Side by side, nobody can call it a lie."

Bren watched her hand move. Steady. His own wasn't, and hers wasn't, he realized, quite as steady as it was pretending to be — there was a pressure in how she held the pen that hadn't been there a minute ago.

"There was one about Kael," he said. "Eleven years back. The Holder before said he'd hold this place together or it would break him."

Ivra's pen stopped. She did not look up.

"I was alone in there with sixty years of people who faded," Bren said. "And the last thing any of them wrote was watching it start to happen to him too."

"And now there are two of us who've read it." She started writing again. "That's worth something. A thing that's only in one head dies with the head. A thing two people know, you can't bury so easy."

He almost laughed, and it came out wrong, closer to the thing the forty-year journal had written about reaching for crying and finding nothing. "The proof was sitting in crates," he said. "The whole time. In the dark. The proof was sitting in crates."

"It is always sitting in crates." Ivra dipped her pen. "That's the part nobody wants to hear. It isn't hidden. Nobody hides it. It just gets packed up and set against a wall, and the wall gets forgotten, and the next lot packs theirs up and sets it next to the first." She finished a line and moved to the next. "Bring me the rest. All of them. We work backward from this year."

Bren stood. His legs had warmed enough to hold him. He went to the door, and stopped, with his hand on the frame.

"How long will it take," he said, "to go through all of it."

Ivra didn't look up from the page. "As long as it takes. Go get the next load."

He went.

</scene>

Does the new draft make the same error — does it assert something that contradicts what was established, in the way described? A draft that simply leaves the fact out does not make the error.

Answer with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"verdict": "reintroduced" | "consistent" | "not_present", "evidence": "<verbatim sentence from the new draft that decides it, or empty for not_present>"}

"reintroduced": the new draft contradicts the established fact.
"consistent": the new draft states the fact and agrees with what was established.
"not_present": the new draft does not touch the fact either way.
